question: Is the proposed elapsed-time temporal relevance adjustment novel, given that TempRALM (arxiv:2401.13222) already combines semantically and temporally relevant documents in a retrieval-augmented LM, and Prior et al. (arxiv:2605.23497) already enforce temporal validity via fact-date extraction and version filtering in statutory QA?
description: TempRALM reports up to 74% improvement by ranking documents by combining semantic and temporal relevance; Prior et al. build a time-sensitive statutory QA benchmark and a RAG variant that filters document versions by extracted fact date. If either already constitutes a retrieval-agnostic elapsed-time re-ranking wrapper over versioned documents, the proposed core mechanism is pre-empted.
rationale: This uncertainty directly determines whether the contribution can stand as stated; it must be resolved before investing in benchmark construction.
resolution: Full-text reading of TempRALM (arxiv:2401.13222) shows the proposed core mechanism is already published: it computes an elapsed-time temporal score tau(q_t,d_t), normalizes it, and sums it with the semantic score (TempRet_t = s(q,d) + tau(q_t,d_t)), explicitly claiming it "could be used to extend any retriever that ranks documents using a numerical similarity score" and requiring no re-indexing. This matches the idea's "retrieval-agnostic semantic + elapsed-time temporal adjustment" almost exactly. Prior et al. (arxiv:2605.23497) additionally show that hard version filtering is the effective mitigation for statutory QA. The remaining open part -- whether a continuous elapsed-time term can beat hard validity-interval filtering specifically on amended regulatory texts -- is tracked as U004.
